def: A collective right of a First Nation to land it occupied before Crown sovereignty. Established by court declaration or agreement, and can only be transferred to the Crown.
Admitting responsibility, for example by a partial payment on a fixed-sum claim or a written confirmation. Restarts both limitation clocks from that date.
Each side presents its own case as strongly as it can, and a neutral judge decides. The judge only sees what the parties put forward.
A change by a life tenant that improves the property, such as adding a deck. Technically waste, but usually no damages are awarded.
The party who brings an appeal.
The local official who decides whether a proposed subdivision is in the public interest and may require road or park dedication and services.
A private process where a neutral arbitrator hears both sides and makes a decision (an award) that is usually binding and final. Common in commercial leases.
A fund run by the LTSA that compensates people who lose land because of the Torrens system or land title office errors. A last resort.
The civil standard of proof: more likely than not. A tie means the plaintiff loses.
A strata development where land, rather than a building, is divided into strata lots. Roads and amenities are usually common property paid for by the owners.
A claim registered against land by an unpaid contractor, subcontractor or worker under the Builders Lien Act. Filed within 45 days of trigger dates; lasts 1 year unless enforced.
A set of restrictive covenants applied to every lot in a development sold by a common vendor, registered under LTA s.220. Common in bare land stratas.
The obligation to prove the case. In a civil case it's on the plaintiff.
A law passed by a municipality, such as a zoning or building bylaw.
The set of facts that gives someone the right to sue.
A registered warning by someone claiming an interest in land, blocking inconsistent dealings. Lapses after 2 months unless a lawsuit is started and a CPL registered.
A notice on title that a lawsuit claiming an interest in the land has started. Formerly called lis pendens.
The official record of a parcel's fee simple owner, legal description and the charges registered against it.
Any registered interest in land less than a fee simple: mortgages, easements, covenants, leases, liens, judgments.
Personal property that isn't attached to land, such as furniture or free-standing equipment. The seller takes it unless the contract says otherwise.
BC's online tribunal for strata disputes (no monetary limit), small claims up to $5,000, motor vehicle claims up to $50,000, and co-op disputes.
Law made by judges through written decisions, built up case by case since medieval England. In the broad sense it includes equity and is contrasted with statute law.
The parts of a strata development not within any strata lot, owned by all the owners as tenants in common.
An agreement between two or more people that creates a legal obligation to do, or not do, something.
An amount the court orders the losing party to pay the winner, set by a tariff. Covers only part of real legal fees, and is at the court's discretion.
Money a court orders one party to pay another as compensation for a wrong.
A judgment against a party who failed to respond within the court's time limits. They lose without a hearing.
The pre-trial process of exchanging evidence: questioning the other side under oath (examination for discovery) and exchanging all relevant documents.
To treat an earlier decision as not binding because a crucial fact is different.
In an easement, the dominant tenement is the land that benefits; the servient tenement is the land that carries the burden.
A paper copy of title issued only on the owner's request since 1979. While it's out, transfers and mortgages can't be registered.
Errors and omissions insurance: professional liability coverage for licensees' mistakes. Requires written notice of any circumstance that could lead to a claim, however weak.
A right to use a neighbour's land in a particular way (a right of way, a drain, light) for the benefit of your own land. Runs with the land if registered.
A claim or burden registered against title, such as a mortgage, lien or judgment.
Flagrant or malicious destruction by a life tenant, such as arson. Not excused by "without impeachment for waste" unless expressly stated.
Principles of fairness developed by the courts of chancery to soften the rigid common law. Where equity and common law conflict, equity wins.
When a person dies with no will and no heirs, their land goes to the Crown.
A bundle of rights to hold land, rather than absolute ownership. Comes from the feudal system; the Crown still holds underlying title.
An estate measured by someone else's life, created when a life tenant sells their life estate. Ends when the original life tenant dies.
Enforcing a judgment by having the sheriff seize and sell the debtor's assets under a writ of execution.
The largest bundle of rights a private person can hold in land. The closest thing to ownership in Canada.
Something attached to land or a building so that it's legally part of the real property. Stays with the property on a sale.
The prescribed Freehold Transfer used to transfer fee simple title in BC. The contract of purchase and sale itself isn't registered.
A court order directing someone who owes the debtor money (an employer or bank) to pay it into court instead. 70% of wages are exempt.
Industrial, Commercial and Investment real estate: offices, retail, industrial, apartments, hotels, development land and businesses.
The Torrens principle that the registered fee simple owner's title is conclusive and can't be defeated, subject to statutory exceptions. Doesn't extend to charges in BC.
An equitable court order telling someone to stop doing something. A mandatory injunction orders them to do something.
Co-ownership with a right of survivorship: when one owner dies, their interest passes to the surviving joint tenants. Needs the four unities of time, title, interest and possession.
The party who owes money under a court judgment, and the party who is owed it.
A court's review of a tribunal's decision, for unfair process (natural justice) or acting outside its jurisdiction.
The power of a court, tribunal or government over particular subjects, places or amounts.
A strata created on land leased for at least 50 years from a leasehold landlord (a government, certain First Nations or a university). Buyers get leases, not fee simple.
Permission to appeal. Required for the Supreme Court of Canada, which can refuse.
Legally responsible.
Personal permission to do something on someone else's land. Not an interest in land, can't be registered and doesn't bind a buyer.
An estate lasting for the life of the life tenant. Registered as a charge. Afterwards the land goes to the remainderman or back to the reversioner.
The time limit for starting a lawsuit. In BC: 2 years from discovery, with a 15-year ultimate limit. Miss it and the right to sue is gone.
The Land Title and Survey Authority of BC, which has run the land title and survey systems since 2005.
A process where a neutral mediator helps the parties reach their own settlement. The mediator doesn't decide anything.
The mortgagor is the borrower who grants the mortgage; the mortgagee is the lender who receives it.
The LTSA's online service (formerly BC OnLine) for searching titles, plans and documents.
Basic fair-process rules, such as the right to be heard and an unbiased decision-maker.
"No one can give what they don't have." At common law, a forged deed broke the chain of title for all later owners.
"Not my deed." A defence that a signer didn't understand the basic nature of what they signed, making the document void.
A substantial and unreasonable interference with someone's use and enjoyment of their land, such as noise, smells or flooding.
"No goods." Marked on a writ of execution when the sheriff finds nothing to seize.
Under the Occupiers Liability Act, anyone in possession of premises or with responsibility for and control over them. There can be several, including a licensee at an open house.
A life tenant letting the property deteriorate by doing nothing. Generally not liable.
Parcel identifier: a permanent 9-digit number for each titled parcel. Found on the property tax notice or BC Assessment.
The party who sues. "Plaintiff" in BC Supreme Court; "claimant" in Small Claims Court.
The formal documents where each side states its case: notice of civil claim, response, reply, counterclaim. Their purpose is to narrow the issues.
A promise to do something, such as pay for maintenance. Generally doesn't run with the land, though an owner can become bound by conduct (Crystal Square).
An earlier court decision that later courts are expected to follow on similar facts.
Law governing disputes between individuals, such as contracts and torts. Also called civil law.
A right to enter someone's land and take something from it, such as timber, gravel or minerals. Can exist without a dominant tenement and can't be implied.
Law involving the state: criminal, tax and constitutional law.
The person who receives the fee simple when a life estate ends, if it doesn't go back to the original grantor.
Law-making power over matters the Constitution doesn't specifically assign. Held by the federal government.
A registered promise not to do something on your land (e.g. not build above 15 feet) for the benefit of neighbouring land. Must be negative in effect.
The original owner who gets the property back when a life estate they created ends.
The feature of joint tenancy where a deceased owner's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenants, outside the will.
A strata document setting each lot's share of the common property, generally used to split the strata's expenses.
A covenant registered under LTA s.219 in favour of the province or a local government. Unlike common law restrictive covenants, it can be positive or negative.
An equitable remedy ordering a party to actually carry out a contract, such as transferring a property. Discretionary and can be lost through delay.
"Let the former decision stand." Courts follow earlier decisions on substantially the same facts.
A written law passed by Parliament, a provincial legislature or a municipal council. Also called legislation.
A right of way under LTA s.218 held by a government, utility or other authorized body. Unlike an ordinary easement, it needs no dominant tenement.
The part of a strata development owned individually, with its own title. Informally a "unit".
The plan deposited at the land title office that creates strata lots and common property.
Dividing land into two or more parcels. In BC it requires compliance with the Land Title Act and approval.
Co-ownership where each owner holds a separate share (which can be unequal) that can be sold or left by will. No right of survivorship. Presumed in BC unless joint tenancy is clearly stated.
Insurance against title defects, fraud and issues like access, zoning and boundaries. A lender's policy protects only the lender.
A land registration system, from South Australia (1858), where title itself is registered and the register is the proof of ownership. Used in BC.
A private wrong, other than breach of contract, that injures someone and for which a court will award damages. Negligence is the most common.
Wrongfully entering, remaining on, or placing something on another person's land, including its airspace or subsurface.
A specialized decision-making body created by statute for one area of disputes. Not part of the court system, but its decisions can be reviewed by the courts.
A person or company holding property in their name for the benefit of someone else (the beneficiary).
The 15-year outer limit for most claims, usually running from the date of the act or omission, whether or not it was discovered.
A document that looks valid but has no legal effect: a forged deed, one for an illegal purpose, or one subject to non est factum.
A life tenant actively damaging or destroying part of the property, such as demolishing a garage. Liable.
Provincial permission to use surface or groundwater under the Water Sustainability Act. Not recorded in the land title office; passes to a buyer with any unpaid fees.
